newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: NATO inaugurates new security body for partners.
newsitem.headline: NATO inaugurates new security body for partners.

text.p: NATO states and 27 partnership countries met on Friday for the first time in a new body created to try to meet the security worries of countries unlikely to gain alliance membership next July.

The Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council (EAPC), which will have a permanent secretariat at NATO's Brussels headquarters, merges the alliance's military cooperation programme and a forum for political dialogue with non-member countries.

Both the alliance's Partnership for Peace (PFP) military cooperation programme and the North Atlantic Cooperation Council (NACC) were created after the collapse of communism to try and fill a security vacuum in central and eastern Europe.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told the opening session the predecessors of the new organisation were born in the rubble of the collapsed Berlin Wall, but now it was time to move forward and forge far closer ties.

"We have moved beyond mere dialogue and cooperation. Today we are aiming at nothing less than the true integration of Europe and the transatlantic community. We are turning a Europe of shared ideals into a Europe of shared responsibilities," she said.

She said the EAPC would be equipped to boost cooperation on a range of issues including arms control and proliferation, terrorism, disaster relief, and a "full range of peace support operations", such as the current peace mission in Bosnia.

"The EAPC is part of a larger structure we are building to prevent future conflicts in Europe," she added, saying it was part of wider efforts to build security structures that do more than just "respond to crises".
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said the meeting in the scenic setting of a baroque monastery in Sintra, Portugal "represented both an end and a new beginning".
"We have moved far beyond where we were in 1991. Cooperation has become a real two-way street," he added.

The new body is seen as a key pillar in a new emerging European security order for the 21st century, taking its place alongside an enlarged NATO, a permanent NATO-Russia Council, and a new security charter with the Ukraine intialled on Thursday.

NATO states, which are set to invite new members to join the Atlantic Alliance at a special summit in Madrid on July 8-9, want the new body to help avoid creating schisms between those countries which win membership and those that do not.

The EAPC, which will develop areas for joint consultation and action and plan joint military exercises, is also intended to keep close links between countries seeking NATO membership and others, like Ukraine, which seek only close ties.
"It will be a place not just for those who aspire to membership in NATO, but for those who choose not to," Albright said.

Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are front-runners to join out of 11 countries from former communist eastern Europe clamouring to gain admittance to the West's defence club, with Slovenia and Romania making late challenges.
At their first formal discussion of which countries should be invited to join at the Madrid summit, NATO countries differed openly over how many old enemies to take in.

The United States, by far NATO's most important member, signalled its desire to keep the number down to three, arguing the need to keep the "highest possible standards", while a southern group of countries favoured five new members.
Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Guterres, the host of the meeting, said the EAPC would provide a critical link in a new "ring of security" embracing north America, Europe, central and north Asia.
"We must have the political will to address the crises that may pose a serious threat to the security and stability of our 'ring'," he told the meeting.

Albright also called on Friday for NATO to send an assessment team to Albania to see how the alliance can help the armed forces in the crisis-wracked Balkan country -- a demonstration of just how volatile the region remains.
